ceip-polder-land-payments-bangladesh.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered six safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, forests, physical cultural property, involuntary resettlement and projects on international waterways. The policy on indigenous peoples was not triggered, because none of the people in the selected polders were found to be from tribal communities (Project Appraisal Document, 29 May 2013). Because the credit was to pay for land acquisition and resettlement costs, a memorandum was prepared seeking approval from the Bank's Regional Vice Presidency for the use of credit proceeds to reimburse those costs. A Social Management and Resettlement Policy Framework and a draft resettlement action plan for the first works package were disclosed on 15 February 2013, and the financing agreement required the borrower to carry out the project in accordance with that framework and the environmental management framework. The implementing agency was the Bangladesh Water Development Board, which prepared each plan, got the Bank's agreement, disclosed it locally and implemented it; 36 grievance redress committees were set up across the first two packages. No construction was to be carried out on a site until land acquisition and compensation there were complete (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 June 2024).

lahore-walled-city-shop-removals.conditions: The project was environmental category A, the category assigned partly because of the substantial resettlement expected in the cultural heritage component. Two instruments governed it: an Environmental and Social Management Framework used to screen the municipal grants, and a Resettlement Framework for the cultural heritage works, under which a Resettlement Action Plan was implemented in the Walled City (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 19 May 2014). The plan set the entitlement matrix on the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy, OP 4.12, and ruled out compensation for anyone who moved onto the site after the cut-off date. It required that compensation be paid about one month before any shop, part of a shop or plot was taken, that no shop or plot be taken without full payment, and that where a claim was disputed the assessed amount be pledged in the affected person's favour until the dispute was decided. Money was to be deposited by the project with the Land Acquisition Collector, who paid the shopkeepers; the construction contractor could start work only after the project took the site over. The executing agency was the Sustainable Development of the Walled City of Lahore Project, with the Revenue Department responsible for assessment, payment and possession (Resettlement Action Plan, March 2010).

nepal-road-sector-unpaid-compensation.conditions: The project was environmental category B and triggered four safeguard policies: environmental assessment, involuntary resettlement, indigenous peoples and forests. A sector-wide Environmental and Social Management Framework was disclosed in Nepal on 7 September 2007, with an initial environmental examination and an environmental management plan required for each road. The Government of Nepal was to be responsible for completing compensation for lost assets to project-affected families before the start of any civil works, while the credit could pay other resettlement and rehabilitation costs under the agreed resettlement action plan. A draft resettlement action plan and environmental management plan for the first year of works were submitted to the Bank on 18 September 2007 and were to be disclosed before the project became effective (Project Appraisal Document, 6 November 2007). The implementing agency was the Department of Roads, whose Geo-Environmental and Social Unit was to monitor impacts after construction.

swat-s3b-road-land-acquisition.conditions: The grant came under the Bank's policy for emergency operations, so the Environmental and Social Screening and Assessment Framework of the Multi Donor Trust Fund applied in place of the usual project-specific safeguard instruments, and the trust fund portfolio as a whole was placed in environmental category B. An environmental impact assessment and environmental management plan were prepared by the supervision consultant for each of the three phases and submitted to the Bank by the implementing agency, the Pakhtunkhwa Highway Authority, and the supervision consultants were contractually bound to implement the management plan. Trust fund money cannot normally pay compensation, so approval was sought from, and given by, the Bank's Regional Vice President to pay compensation for lost assets and lost production from the grant. The right of way was held to the minimum the design required in order to limit the loss of houses and shops, and grievance redress committees made up of affected people handled disputes over ownership, amounts and late payment. The Highway Authority also engaged auditors to review the land acquisition procedure and outcome for all three phases (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 11 August 2016).

siddhirganj-pipeline-transmission-land.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered two safeguard policies: environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. Cleared environmental and social assessments, environmental management plans and resettlement action plans were conditions of loan negotiations. Compensation was set by the national Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance of 1982 together with the Bank's resettlement policy, OP 4.12, and both the amounts due under national law and any amounts payable above them were to be funded by the two implementing companies, Gas Transmission Company Limited and Power Grid Company of Bangladesh, rather than by the credit. Losses were to be assessed by a Compensation Determination Committee including a representative of the affected people and of an NGO; the company was then to deposit the money with the Deputy Commissioner of the district, who paid landowners by account payee cheque. The appraisal document states plainly that no civil works were to start before affected people had been given their compensation and entitlements, and required the list of affected people and the amounts to be published on both companies' websites (Project Appraisal Document, 7 October 2008).

gujarat-highway-ii-delayed-compensation.conditions: The project was classified category A and triggered five safeguard policies: environmental assessment, forests, physical cultural resources, indigenous peoples and involuntary resettlement. Resettlement action plans were prepared for the eight widening corridors and an Indigenous People's Development Plan for the corridors through Schedule V tribal areas, with free, prior and informed consultation held there; drafts of the resettlement policy framework, the action plans and the development plans were published by the state Roads and Buildings Department and by the Bank. The framework set compensation for land at market value and structures at replacement cost, provided shifting and transitional allowances and income generation assistance, extended replacement cost and time to remove assets to people without title, and required the amounts to be updated every year. All land acquisition and resettlement costs paid in cash were to come from Government of Gujarat funds, with loan money paying only for the consultancies, goods and works needed to carry the plans out. Loan covenants required Gujarat to obtain every necessary permit and clearance before civil works started on any road, to report quarterly on safeguard compliance, and to maintain a district-level grievance redress mechanism for resettlement and rehabilitation (Project Appraisal Document, 7 November 2013).

dehlon-bypass-uncompensated-landowner.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered four safeguard policies: environmental assessment, physical cultural resources, forests and involuntary resettlement. A Resettlement and Rehabilitation Policy Framework with an entitlement matrix was adopted, and resettlement action plans were completed and disclosed for the first phase of roads before appraisal. Two covenants governed the land. The Government of Punjab was to ensure that works were carried out in line with the framework and the plans, and that neither was revised or set aside without the Bank's prior approval. It was also not to begin any civil works at an affected site until the physical relocation of people at that site had been completed to the Bank's satisfaction, with relocation on all first-phase roads to be finished before 5 June 2008 (Project Appraisal Document, 10 November 2006). The implementing agency was the Punjab Roads and Bridges Development Board.

salem-tnudp-squatter-resettlement.conditions: Because the money was lent on to many separate sub-projects, the safeguard policies were applied through an Environmental and Social Framework rather than fixed in advance: the framework's screening tools decided, sub-project by sub-project, which policies applied and what plan was needed. The framework was in place by appraisal, was formally approved by a Government of Tamil Nadu order, and was treated as meeting the requirements of the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy, OP 4.12. At appraisal the project was recorded as triggering environmental assessment, cultural property and involuntary resettlement (Project Appraisal Document, 25 May 2005). For the Chennai transport works, consultants prepared the environmental management plan and resettlement action plan, the state financing company reviewed and approved them, and the Bank then had to issue a no-objection before the works could be put out to bid; a works contract could be signed only once the land was clear and the resettlement plan had been fully carried out. The implementing agencies were Tamil Nadu Urban Infrastructure Financial Services and, for the transport works, the Chennai Metropolitan Development Authority, and two environmental and social audits were carried out during implementation (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 September 2014).

assam-roads-uncompensated-acquisition.conditions: The project triggered six safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, forests, physical cultural resources, indigenous peoples and involuntary resettlement. The state government endorsed a resettlement and rehabilitation policy and entitlement matrix consistent with the Bank's policy; a resettlement policy framework guided later phases, and the action plans for the four first-phase upgrading works were disclosed in Assam on 19 July 2011 and by the Bank on 27 July 2011. A separate Indigenous Peoples Development Plan was prepared for the first and second phase roads. The Public Works Roads Department was to staff an Environment and Social Cell to carry the plans out and engage a local NGO to help; construction supervision consultants were to monitor that work and an independent consultant to evaluate it at mid-term and at the end (Project Appraisal Document, 17 February 2012). When land and property on one works package were taken without compensation, in breach of the agreed plan, work on that package was suspended until the process was completed and the compensation money transferred (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 25 March 2020).

drc-selembao-loange-compensation.conditions: The project was environmental category A, but because the sub-project sites were not known at approval the remaining policies, including involuntary resettlement, were left to be applied case by case through a programmatic process of screening, assessment, consultation, disclosure and approval run over the life of the project; an environmental consulting firm was hired to manage the environmental and social management plan and reviewed every infrastructure sub-project, including those already approved (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 29 October 2010). For the Loange bridge, a resettlement and compensation plan was prepared under OP 4.12 and under the commitments in the project's financing agreement, and it states that the plan had to be carried out before the infrastructure works began. The plan records the government's formal undertaking to respect the compensation rights of everyone affected, fixes a cut-off date for eligibility, and provides that payment comes before work starts. The list of eligible households was agreed by all parties on 12 March 2008. Implementation was to be handled by an independent national or regional expert recruited by the delegated project owner, BCMI, assisted by a resettlement committee including the road agency, the environmental firm, village committees and local authorities (Plan de réinstallation et de compensation, May 2008).

ghana-urban-water-unpaid-compensation.conditions: The project was environmental category B and triggered four safeguard policies: environmental assessment, involuntary resettlement, safety of dams and projects on international waterways. An environmental assessment management plan for the first package of works, a resettlement policy framework for the whole project and a dam safety report were prepared before appraisal, and project staff were given resettlement training so they could prepare resettlement action plans for individual works during construction. A dated covenant added when the project was restructured required the borrower to set up an escrow account used only for compensation and disturbance allowances to project-affected persons, for full compensation before works were implemented. The account was opened on time but was never funded on time, and the borrower's failure to pay full compensation costs is listed as a major implementation issue. The implementing agency was Ghana Water Company Limited (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 21 December 2016).

burkina-donsin-airport-roads-resettlemen.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered three safeguard policies: environmental assessment, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement, all three because of the land the access road works would take. The environmental and social impact assessment and its management plan were disclosed by the Bank on 22 October 2012 and in Burkina Faso on 19 November 2012, and the resettlement action plan on 19 February 2013 and 19 November 2012; both were to be carried out before the road construction works actually started, and the plans for the airport works were to be substantially carried out before the road works began. Measures agreed to in the plan included new village sites with schools, health clinics and wells, improved houses, cash compensation for one year of lost farm income and training in intensive farming, and the resettlement sites were chosen with the affected people, the host communities and the local administrations. The government provided the money for the plan and implementation had already begun at appraisal. A condition required the implementing agency, the Donsin airport project authority (MOAD), to adopt within three months a manual of procedures covering the impact assessment, the management plan and the resettlement plan, and not to change it without the Bank's written consent (Project Appraisal Document, 22 April 2013).

rwanda-rssp2-marshland-resettlement.conditions: The project triggered five safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, pest management, involuntary resettlement and projects on international waterways; under the last of these the Bank sent riparian notifications to the Nile and Lake Tanganyika basin countries on 5 May 2008. Because the sites were not known at preparation, an Environmental and Social Management Framework with a screening tool was prepared and applied to each funding request, and a Resettlement Policy Framework disclosed in January 2008 set the rules for preparing a resettlement action plan for any sub-project that displaced people or cut their access to resources (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 April 2013). Thirteen such plans were prepared and carried out, for named dams, irrigation channels and marshlands. Compensation followed the valuations of crops and property, article 29 of the Rwandan Constitution, the Expropriation Law No. 18/2007 of 19 April 2007 and OP 4.12; districts gave land in exchange for land to farmers displaced from state-owned marshlands, and the project supplied building materials for houses in the grouped settlements. The plans were implemented by the project and the districts under the Ministry of Agriculture and Animal Resources, with a project unit coordinating and district staff passing grievances to its safeguards specialists (Resettlement Implementation Completion Report for RSSP2, July 2012).

south-west-roads-turkestan-sairam-compen.conditions: When the lending instrument was changed at appraisal, the whole project was reclassified as environmental category A involving involuntary resettlement, which meant the Bank's own policies required a full environmental assessment and resettlement action plans to be completed and disclosed before appraisal. Instead a waiver of that requirement was sought from the Board of Executive Directors in a request dated 6 October 2008, on the understanding that the assessment and a resettlement policy framework would be finished before the project went to the Board and that the site-specific management plans and resettlement action plans would be prepared during construction; the earlier framework documents were withdrawn from the Bank's InfoShop. The resettlement action plan for South Kazakhstan Region of March 2011 committed the borrower to compensate land users without formal title on the same terms as people with title, and its entitlement matrix gave long-term leaseholders of state-owned arable land cash compensation based on the market value of a three-year average gross yield, payment for trees and fixed assets, and a renewed lease on an alternative plot, whatever the severity of the loss. That last provision was missing from the Kazakh and Russian version of the matrix handed out in the project leaflet, and people in Sairam said they had never seen the leaflet (Inspection Panel Report and Recommendation, 18 October 2011). The implementing agency was the Committee for Roads, which depended on local authorities, the Akimats, for documents and for paying compensation (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 19 June 2025).

hanoi-ring-road-2-relocation.conditions: The project was classified category A under the Bank's environmental assessment policy, which was the only environmental safeguard policy triggered, the category reflecting the scale of land acquisition and the building of a resettlement site in a built-up area. It also triggered the involuntary resettlement policy, OP 4.12. A resettlement policy framework and resettlement action plan were prepared in line with Vietnamese law and Bank policy and disclosed at preparation, and the plan was updated and disclosed again at the first restructuring. Resettlement was run through bodies at city, district and ward level, the project management unit carried out the plan on behalf of the Hanoi People's Committee, and an outside agency monitored it independently, reporting every three months after the first restructuring instead of every six. The mid-term review found the project unit and the district authorities were following the city's own rules rather than the agreed framework and plan: they were using an earlier cut-off date set by the Land Law, refusing help for land held without permission, paying less than replacement cost, and giving no assistance to unregistered businesses (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 18 January 2018).

bahia-viver-melhor-ii-resettlement.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered four safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, because some works were in protected areas, cultural property, to keep sacred sites in Salvador undisturbed, and involuntary resettlement. A resettlement framework was prepared, with an action plan for the Alagados VI sub-project in Salvador, and the state environmental agency required the implementing company to set up an environmental group and trained its members in environmental analysis (Independent Evaluation Group, ICR Review, 11 June 2014). Households being moved out of high-risk ground were to be offered three options: cash compensation, assisted purchase of a replacement house with the project monitoring the purchase, or a move into a newly built house, with new housing kept within one kilometre of the old homes. Where no agreement was reached on any of the options the case went to court for judicial compensation. The implementing agencies were the state urban development company CONDER and the state urban development secretariat SEDUR (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 April 2014).

rurrenabaque-airport-land-compensation.conditions: The project was environmental category B, partial assessment, and triggered six safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, forest management, indigenous peoples, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement, with the matching safeguard instruments prepared to the Bank's requirements. The airport component was carried out first by the state air navigation agency AASANA and, after that agency was dissolved on 1 December 2021, by a new agency, NAABOL, while the road component stayed with the Bolivian Road Administration, ABC. Compensation for the land taken to extend the airport perimeter was financed not by the credit but by the local government, which had expropriated the land from two owners before the Bank became involved. On finding that payment was outstanding because the local government and the owners did not agree on the amount, the Bank hired a third party to assess the situation and to help bring the valuation of the assets into line with the safeguard policies then in force. Civil works on the airport did not start until May 2018, after the compensation question was settled in January 2018 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 31 May 2024).

philippines-nrimp2-unpaid-land-claims.conditions: The project was environmental category B and triggered three safeguard policies: environmental assessment, involuntary resettlement and indigenous peoples. All the road sub-projects had been identified at appraisal and were to follow the Social and Environmental Management System, and the implementing agency, the Department of Public Works and Highways, already had a land acquisition, resettlement, rehabilitation and indigenous peoples' policy framework that the Bank accepted as consistent with OP 4.12 and OP 4.10 (Independent Evaluation Group, ICR Review, 20 November 2017). Bank policy required compensation claims to be paid before construction was allowed to begin, and it applied to linked road works built with government money next to the roads the loan paid for, not only to the loan-funded works themselves. Compliance was to be monitored by multi-partite teams set up between the project management office, the department's Environmental and Social Safeguard Office and its regional and district offices, an arrangement that was slow to come together. After the unpaid claims on the linked works came to light, the Bank and the safeguard office agreed an action plan, which included cutting the right of way back to the width actually used so that less land was needed (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 21 June 2017).
